registers.name_in_paper: The State's Sales and Valuation Registry
the Population Registry and other relevant registries
variables_mentioned: unemployment (at least 6 months in a year)

registers.name_in_paper: the 2015-2018 Consumer Expenditure Surveys (CEX, United States)
registers.role: outcomes (US expenditure comparison, Appendix Table A-5)

linkages: individual-level register records with household linkages, allowing the authors to follow the universe of Danish households for almost two decades
women linked to partners: home ownership is defined as the woman, her partner, or both being a home owner, and family income is the sum for woman + partner
women linked to their births and to their children's hospital and ER records
homes linked to women through The State's Sales and Valuation Registry; each woman is assigned the first house she is seen to purchase
homes grouped into year/municipality/housing-type/valuation-quartile clusters to compute the SPAR-style valuation correction factor

sample.universe: Danish women aged 20-44 in the register data who were not home owners at the beginning of 1992-1993 and who first purchased a home between 1993 and 2004 at ages 18-42
sample.unit_of_observation: woman-year (child-level for the infant and early-childhood health outcomes)
selection_rules: houses and apartments with residential use, 1992-2006 (20,993,937 house-years)
non-negative public valuation; non-negative sales price; a single address; private use only
at least five houses sold in the cluster
sales price at least 40% and less than 300% of the public valuation
only normal sales between individuals (e.g. sales between family members excluded)
either woman or partner owns a single house, individually or jointly (1,476,288)
first purchased a house between 1993 and 2005 (216,906)
sufficient data to calculate lagged one-year house price changes (214,451; this screen drops 18 and 19 year olds and omits the first two years of the treatment period)
non-missing household income (211,975); non-missing house price and ownership (207,127)
sufficient data to calculate the municipality correction factor (207,016)
purchased a house whose public valuation changed by less than 50% in the prior year (199,964)
exclude those in the 1st and 99th percentile of the lagged one-year house price change (198,435)
women whose partners purchased a home after 1993 but before the woman and partner became a couple are omitted
individuals who moved out of their newly purchased home before the end of the year are not included
sample.period: register data 1992-2011; fertility analysis 1995-2006, with the sample period expanded accordingly for health outcomes in the first year of life and at ages 1-5
sample.n_observations: 1,105,559 woman-years (Table 3 and the baseline fertility models); 125,903 children (125,291 with non-missing birth weight)

construction_notes: Home value HV is estimated as in Equation (1): the public valuation of the home times the mean over- or undervaluation of houses actually sold in the same year/municipality/housing-type/valuation-quartile cluster, weighted by the woman's and her partner's ownership shares (a method similar to the equal-weighted sale price appraisal ratio, SPAR, index of Bourassa et al. 2006).
Each woman is assigned the HV of the first house she is seen to purchase, regardless of later moves; the authors describe this as the reduced form of an IV model using first-home price changes.
The main independent variable is the once-lagged one-year change, HV_{t-1} - HV_{t-2}; Table 4 also uses two-, three- and four-year lagged changes.

All monetary variables are in 100,000 Danish Kroner deflated to 2006 prices using the CPI; the 2006 exchange rate was approximately 0.17 USD/DKK, or 0.12 adjusting for purchasing power parity, and the PPP rate is used for international comparisons (100,000 DKK is about $12,000).

Public valuations occur in January of the prior year until the end of 2003 and in October of the prior year afterwards; all privately owned properties are valued in uneven years and adjusted in even years.
The number of inpatient days excludes the admission related to the childbirth and the following four days.
Fertility models use births in 1995-2006; health models expand the sample period accordingly.
Income quartiles are defined over the full sample period (footnote 27).
Table 2 reports predicted outcomes obtained from the main specification estimated without the lagged one-year home value change or fixed effects.

Predicted Prematurity and Predicted Low BW in Table 7 are predicted values from a regression of each dependent variable on age, years of education, number of children, household income and partner status.

Standard errors are clustered at the municipality level throughout the Danish analysis; each woman's municipality is fixed at the location of her first purchased home, so household clusters are subsumed.

claims.statement: A 100,000 DKK increase in the lagged one-year home value increases the likelihood of giving birth by 0.16 percentage points among first-time homeowner women aged 20-44 (Table 3 column 1: year and municipality fixed effects only).

treatment.label: Lagged one-year home value change (100,000 DKK)

register_source.value: The State's Sales and Valuation Registry (public valuations, sales prices, ownership, housing type); no register variable names given

definition.value: Once-lagged one-year change in the woman's estimated home value, dHV_{i,t-1} = HV_{i,t-1} - HV_{i,t-2}. HV is the SPAR-style estimated market value of Equation (1): the public valuation of the home times the mean over- or undervaluation of homes actually sold in the same year/municipality/housing-type/valuation-quartile cluster, summed over the woman's and her partner's ownership shares. Each woman is assigned the value of the first house she is seen to purchase, regardless of whether she later moves. Expressed in 100,000 DKK, CPI-deflated to 2006 prices.

timing.value: one-year change measured from t-2 to t-1, i.e. the year before the outcome year t ('once-lagged one-year change')

register_source.value: Birth Registry (all hospital and home births in Denmark); no register variable names given

definition.value: Indicator for whether woman i gave birth in year t, constructed from the Birth Registry

timing.value: calendar year t, the year after the one-year home value change

units.value: change in the probability (0-1 scale) per 100,000 DKK increase in the lagged one-year home value; multiply by 100 for percentage points

magnitude.interpretation: 1.34% increase relative to the mean fertility rate of 0.1166; significant at the 10% level

estimand.target_population: women aged 20-44 in Denmark who first purchased a home between 1993 and 2004 (the woman, her partner, or both being the owner)
estimand.time_horizon: likelihood of giving birth in the year following the one-year home value change
estimand.formal_query: E[Birth | do(dHV_{t-1}=h+1)] - E[Birth | do(dHV_{t-1}=h)], in 100,000 DKK units, for the homeowner population

population.description: Women aged 20-44 in Denmark who were not home owners at the beginning of 1992-1993 and who first purchased a home between 1993 and 2004 at ages 18-42 (the woman, her partner, or both being the owner)
subgroups_defined: family income quartile (defined over the full sample period)
population.selection: conditioned on first home purchase between 1993 and 2004 at ages 18-42 by the woman or her partner, on the home-level screens of Appendix Table A-1 (normal sales, clusters with at least five sales, sales price between 40% and 300% of the public valuation, valuation change below 50%, 1st and 99th percentile of lagged one-year price change excluded) and on complete data on income, home price and ownership

identification.source_of_variation: Short-run (once-lagged one-year) variation in the estimated market value of the first home a woman purchased, net of municipality-by-year and age-of-purchase-by-year-of-purchase fixed effects; Danish housing market 1993-2006, including the boom of the early- to mid-2000s

key_assumptions.assumption: Changes in home prices are unrelated to unobserved characteristics that also correlate with the likelihood of giving birth and with birth outcomes (conditional ignorability given the fixed effects and observed controls)
key_assumptions.supported_by: Table 2: average observable characteristics and thirteen predicted outcomes are remarkably similar across quartiles of the lagged one-year home price change

key_assumptions.assumption: There are no contemporaneous, unobserved shocks in municipalities that are correlated both with the timing, magnitude and sign of home price changes and with fertility outcomes
key_assumptions.supported_by: renter placebo: the effect of municipality-wide home price changes on renter fertility is very small and not statistically significant (Table 4, column 1); municipality-by-year fixed effects absorb municipality-year shocks

key_assumptions.assumption: The price change of the first home purchased is the relevant exposure even for women who move; conceptually the first home's price change instruments the actual price change experienced and the reported estimates are the reduced form of that IV model
key_assumptions.supported_by: low mobility rates in Denmark; women are kept in the sample after moving and keep the price changes of their first home

key_assumptions.assumption: The estimation sample is conditioned on becoming a first-time home owner: women who were not home owners at the beginning of 1992-1993 and who purchased a home between 1993 and 2004 at ages 18-42 (plus the home-level screens of Appendix Table A-1)
key_assumptions.supported_by: Appendix Table A-1 lists the observations dropped by each screen

key_assumptions.assumption: The effect of a home value change is linear in the size of the change, so one coefficient describes increases and decreases of any size
key_assumptions.supported_by: Section 5.2 interacts the home price change with an indicator for a price decline and finds roughly equal and opposite effects, which the authors read as symmetry

threats_discussed: endogenous choice of home ownership, fertility and child investment decisions
unobserved municipality-by-year shocks correlated with home prices and fertility (e.g. local business cycle variation, changes to municipality services such as child care)
procyclical fertility behaviour
mechanical bias from the interaction of a housing tenure effect and an age-of-purchase effect
endogenous mobility of parents
public valuations may not precisely reflect market values
compositional change in which women give birth (for the infant health outcomes)
robustness_checks: renter placebo sample (Table 4, column 1)
woman fixed effects (Table 4, column 2)
two-, three- and four-year lagged home price changes (Table 4, columns 3-5)
aligning the timing of home price valuation and conception (Table 4, column 6)
balance of observable characteristics and of thirteen predicted outcomes across quartiles of the lagged home price change (Table 2)
alternative sets of controls and fixed effects (Appendix Tables A-3 and A-4)
including women who purchased a home prior to 1993 (footnote 23)
interaction with an indicator for a home price decline, testing symmetry (Section 5.2)
unresolved_confounders: that higher-fertility households, or those with better underlying infant health, are better at predicting future home price growth when they purchase a home in a way uncorrelated with the observables, the age at purchase and the year of purchase
other characteristics the authors cannot control for that change with home prices and can be related to underlying fertility (footnote 33)

links.pointer_quote: Using rich population register data among women aged 20-44 who own a home, we find that for each 100,000 DKK increase in home prices (equivalent to $12,000), the likelihood of giving birth increases by 0.27 percentage points or 2.32%.
They find an effect of 2.11% for each $12,000 of home price increase, which is very close to the 2.32% effect we document in Denmark.

heterogeneity.finding: The least responsive group in percent terms are those aged 25-29 (1.47%), while the most responsive group is those aged 35-39 (2.89%); the effect is not statistically significant for 20-24 or 40-44 year olds (Table 5 Panel A).

The effect is largest for first-time mothers (0.0056, 3.65% of the mean) and statistically significant for women with one and two existing children, but not for those with 3 or more (Table 5 Panel B).
Women in the middle of the income distribution are most responsive; the bottom-quartile estimate is not statistically significant (Table 5 Panel C).
Little evidence of heterogeneity: the effects are similarly sized and statistically significant in all four quartiles (Table 5 Panel D).
Estimates of 0.0038(0.0006) for a 100,000 DKK increase and -0.0040(0.0017) for a 100,000 DKK decrease: roughly equal and opposite, which the authors read as symmetry (Section 5.2).

register_source.value: The State's Sales and Valuation Registry (public valuations, sales prices, ownership, housing type); no register variable names given

definition.value: Once-lagged one-year change in the woman's estimated home value, dHV_{i,t-1} = HV_{i,t-1} - HV_{i,t-2}. HV is the SPAR-style estimated market value of Equation (1): the public valuation of the home times the mean over- or undervaluation of homes actually sold in the same year/municipality/housing-type/valuation-quartile cluster, summed over the woman's and her partner's ownership shares. Each woman is assigned the value of the first house she is seen to purchase, regardless of whether she later moves. Expressed in 100,000 DKK, CPI-deflated to 2006 prices.

timing.value: one-year change measured from t-2 to t-1, i.e. the year before the outcome year t ('once-lagged one-year change')

register_source.value: Birth Registry (all hospital and home births in Denmark); no register variable names given

definition.value: Predicted value from a regression of prematurity on age, years of education, number of children, household income, and partner status, measured in the year of birth

timing.value: in the year of birth

units.value: change in the probability (0-1 scale) per 100,000 DKK increase in the lagged one-year home value; multiply by 100 for percentage points

magnitude.interpretation: statistically significant at the 1% level; the authors read the whole table as showing that home price increases shift the composition of births towards older, more educated, higher income and two-parent households, and that the predicted-outcome estimates are of similar magnitude to the treatment effects in Table 6, confirming that at least some of the health effects are driven by composition

estimand.target_population: mothers who give birth in the first-time homeowner sample
estimand.time_horizon: measured in the year of birth

population.description: Women aged 20-44 in Denmark who were not home owners at the beginning of 1992-1993 and who first purchased a home between 1993 and 2004 at ages 18-42 (the woman, her partner, or both being the owner); restricted to women from the main analysis sample who give birth; multiple births excluded
subgroups_defined: family income quartile (defined over the full sample period)
population.selection: conditioned on first home purchase between 1993 and 2004 at ages 18-42 by the woman or her partner, on the home-level screens of Appendix Table A-1 (normal sales, clusters with at least five sales, sales price between 40% and 300% of the public valuation, valuation change below 50%, 1st and 99th percentile of lagged one-year price change excluded) and on complete data on income, home price and ownership; conditioned on giving birth

identification.source_of_variation: Short-run (once-lagged one-year) variation in the estimated market value of the first home a woman purchased, net of municipality-by-year and age-of-purchase-by-year-of-purchase fixed effects; Danish housing market 1993-2006, including the boom of the early- to mid-2000s

key_assumptions.assumption: Changes in home prices are unrelated to unobserved characteristics that also correlate with the likelihood of giving birth and with birth outcomes (conditional ignorability given the fixed effects and observed controls)
key_assumptions.supported_by: Table 2: average observable characteristics and thirteen predicted outcomes are remarkably similar across quartiles of the lagged one-year home price change

key_assumptions.assumption: There are no contemporaneous, unobserved shocks in municipalities that are correlated both with the timing, magnitude and sign of home price changes and with fertility outcomes
key_assumptions.supported_by: renter placebo: the effect of municipality-wide home price changes on renter fertility is very small and not statistically significant (Table 4, column 1); municipality-by-year fixed effects absorb municipality-year shocks

key_assumptions.assumption: The mechanical bias from housing tenure interacted with age at purchase (longer-tenured and younger buyers are both more exposed to price changes and more likely to give birth) is fully accounted for by age-of-purchase-by-year-of-purchase fixed effects
key_assumptions.supported_by: comparison of estimates with and without these fixed effects (Table 3 columns 2 and 3; Table A-3)

key_assumptions.assumption: The price change of the first home purchased is the relevant exposure even for women who move; conceptually the first home's price change instruments the actual price change experienced and the reported estimates are the reduced form of that IV model
key_assumptions.supported_by: low mobility rates in Denmark; women are kept in the sample after moving and keep the price changes of their first home

key_assumptions.assumption: The estimation sample is conditioned on becoming a first-time home owner: women who were not home owners at the beginning of 1992-1993 and who purchased a home between 1993 and 2004 at ages 18-42 (plus the home-level screens of Appendix Table A-1)
key_assumptions.supported_by: Appendix Table A-1 lists the observations dropped by each screen

key_assumptions.assumption: The effect of a home value change is linear in the size of the change, so one coefficient describes increases and decreases of any size
key_assumptions.supported_by: Section 5.2 interacts the home price change with an indicator for a price decline and finds roughly equal and opposite effects, which the authors read as symmetry

key_assumptions.assumption: Health outcomes are estimated conditional on giving birth, so the sample of births is itself a function of home prices; the authors concede that most of the health effects at birth reflect this change in composition
key_assumptions.supported_by: Table 7 regressions of maternal characteristics and of predicted prematurity / predicted low birth weight on home price changes; mother fixed effects estimates

threats_discussed: endogenous choice of home ownership, fertility and child investment decisions
unobserved municipality-by-year shocks correlated with home prices and fertility (e.g. local business cycle variation, changes to municipality services such as child care)
procyclical fertility behaviour
mechanical bias from the interaction of a housing tenure effect and an age-of-purchase effect
endogenous mobility of parents
public valuations may not precisely reflect market values
compositional change in which women give birth (for the infant health outcomes)
robustness_checks: renter placebo sample (Table 4, column 1)
woman fixed effects (Table 4, column 2)
two-, three- and four-year lagged home price changes (Table 4, columns 3-5)
aligning the timing of home price valuation and conception (Table 4, column 6)
balance of observable characteristics and of thirteen predicted outcomes across quartiles of the lagged home price change (Table 2)
alternative sets of controls and fixed effects (Appendix Tables A-3 and A-4)
including women who purchased a home prior to 1993 (footnote 23)
interaction with an indicator for a home price decline, testing symmetry (Section 5.2)
unresolved_confounders: that higher-fertility households, or those with better underlying infant health, are better at predicting future home price growth when they purchase a home in a way uncorrelated with the observables, the age at purchase and the year of purchase
other characteristics the authors cannot control for that change with home prices and can be related to underlying fertility (footnote 33)

estimation.specification: OLS of the maternal characteristic measured in the year of birth on the once-lagged one-year home value change, with municipality-by-year and age-of-purchase-by-year-of-purchase fixed effects and no other controls; standard errors clustered at the municipality level
fixed_effects: age of purchase x year of purchase

source_table.value: Table 7, column (6)

mediators_claimed: changes in the composition of births: home price increases lead more-advantaged women (older, more educated, higher income, two-parent) to give birth, and the authors conclude these composition effects can explain most of the health effects at birth
ambiguities: The paper prints Equation (2) only for the fertility (Birth) model; the model for this outcome is described in prose as the same specification, so functional_form is left null rather than reconstructed.

theory_referenced: household utility maximization with children and child health as normal goods
credit constraints and consumption smoothing around childbirth

claims.statement: Among mothers aged 35-39, a 100,000 DKK increase in the lagged one-year home value does not significantly change the likelihood of prematurity (Appendix Table A-6, Panel A: Mother's Age, column 4).

treatment.label: Lagged one-year home value change (100,000 DKK)

register_source.value: The State's Sales and Valuation Registry (public valuations, sales prices, ownership, housing type); no register variable names given

definition.value: Once-lagged one-year change in the woman's estimated home value, dHV_{i,t-1} = HV_{i,t-1} - HV_{i,t-2}. HV is the SPAR-style estimated market value of Equation (1): the public valuation of the home times the mean over- or undervaluation of homes actually sold in the same year/municipality/housing-type/valuation-quartile cluster, summed over the woman's and her partner's ownership shares. Each woman is assigned the value of the first house she is seen to purchase, regardless of whether she later moves. Expressed in 100,000 DKK, CPI-deflated to 2006 prices.

timing.value: one-year change measured from t-2 to t-1, i.e. the year before the outcome year t ('once-lagged one-year change')

register_source.value: Birth Registry (all hospital and home births in Denmark); no register variable names given

definition.value: Indicator for gestational age less than 37 completed weeks, from the Birth Registry; conditional on giving birth, multiple births excluded

timing.value: at birth

units.value: change in the probability (0-1 scale) per 100,000 DKK increase in the lagged one-year home value; multiply by 100 for percentage points

magnitude.interpretation: the authors describe the Appendix Table A-6 estimates as imprecise but economically significant for the youngest and oldest mothers, new mothers and those with 3 or more children

estimand.target_population: children born to first-time homeowner mothers aged 35-39
estimand.formal_query: E[Y | do(dHV_{t-1}=h+1)] - E[Y | do(dHV_{t-1}=h)] among births, in 100,000 DKK units

population.description: Women aged 20-44 in Denmark who were not home owners at the beginning of 1992-1993 and who first purchased a home between 1993 and 2004 at ages 18-42 (the woman, her partner, or both being the owner); conditional on giving birth (multiple births excluded), restricted to mothers aged 35-39
subgroups_defined: family income quartile (defined over the full sample period)
population.selection: conditioned on first home purchase between 1993 and 2004 at ages 18-42 by the woman or her partner, on the home-level screens of Appendix Table A-1 (normal sales, clusters with at least five sales, sales price between 40% and 300% of the public valuation, valuation change below 50%, 1st and 99th percentile of lagged one-year price change excluded) and on complete data on income, home price and ownership; conditioned on giving birth and on the subgroup restriction

identification.source_of_variation: Short-run (once-lagged one-year) variation in the estimated market value of the first home a woman purchased, net of municipality-by-year and age-of-purchase-by-year-of-purchase fixed effects; Danish housing market 1993-2006, including the boom of the early- to mid-2000s

key_assumptions.assumption: There are no contemporaneous, unobserved shocks in municipalities that are correlated both with the timing, magnitude and sign of home price changes and with fertility outcomes
key_assumptions.supported_by: renter placebo: the effect of municipality-wide home price changes on renter fertility is very small and not statistically significant (Table 4, column 1); municipality-by-year fixed effects absorb municipality-year shocks

key_assumptions.assumption: The mechanical bias from housing tenure interacted with age at purchase (longer-tenured and younger buyers are both more exposed to price changes and more likely to give birth) is fully accounted for by age-of-purchase-by-year-of-purchase fixed effects
key_assumptions.supported_by: comparison of estimates with and without these fixed effects (Table 3 columns 2 and 3; Table A-3)

key_assumptions.assumption: The price change of the first home purchased is the relevant exposure even for women who move; conceptually the first home's price change instruments the actual price change experienced and the reported estimates are the reduced form of that IV model
key_assumptions.supported_by: low mobility rates in Denmark; women are kept in the sample after moving and keep the price changes of their first home

key_assumptions.assumption: The estimation sample is conditioned on becoming a first-time home owner: women who were not home owners at the beginning of 1992-1993 and who purchased a home between 1993 and 2004 at ages 18-42 (plus the home-level screens of Appendix Table A-1)
key_assumptions.supported_by: Appendix Table A-1 lists the observations dropped by each screen

key_assumptions.assumption: The effect of a home value change is linear in the size of the change, so one coefficient describes increases and decreases of any size
key_assumptions.supported_by: Section 5.2 interacts the home price change with an indicator for a price decline and finds roughly equal and opposite effects, which the authors read as symmetry

key_assumptions.assumption: Health outcomes are estimated conditional on giving birth, so the sample of births is itself a function of home prices; the authors concede that most of the health effects at birth reflect this change in composition

definition.value: Once-lagged one-year change in the woman's estimated home value, dHV_{i,t-1} = HV_{i,t-1} - HV_{i,t-2}.
